title: Africa’s governments already treat the internet as protest infrastructure. Its courts have not caught up
sourceTitle: Africa’s governments already treat the internet as protest infrastructure. Its courts have not caught up
headline: Africa's courts lag on internet protests

pages.text: Governments in Africa often stop the internet when people protest. In July 2025, Angola shut down its internet because people were unhappy about fuel prices. At least 22 people were killed according to the authorities’ own figures; civil society monitors counted 30 dead and more than 1,500 arrested. Experts have tracked these problems since 2014.

pages.text: They found more than 70 separate episodes across 32 countries since 2014, with cases in every year. Access Now’s KeepItOn coalition counted independently and arrived at the same number. Governments use two main ways to stop people. First, they punish one person for what they post online. Second, they turn off the whole network to stop groups from meeting.

Many people think the internet is only about free speech. However, it is also about the right to meet in groups. Courts often look at free speech laws, but they should also look at laws about assembly. If the internet is off, people cannot organize. It is time for courts to protect the right to use the internet for protests.

evidence: On a Saturday in late July 2025, Angola shut down its internet for the first time in its recorded history.
At least 22 people were killed according to the authorities’ own figures; civil society monitors counted 30 dead and more than 1,500 arrested .

Counting only entries where a government restricted, throttled or cut a network itself, and setting aside closures of individual broadcasters, I found more than 70 separate episodes across 32 countries, every year since 2014.

pages.text: Across Africa, governments increasingly treat the internet as infrastructure for protest, yet judicial systems have struggled to keep pace with this reality. In July 2025, Angola experienced its first recorded internet shutdown during protests over rising fuel costs.
pages.caption: Kenya High Court building

imageProvenance.credit: Kenya Judiciary building. Image by Wing via Wikimedia Commons ().

pages.text: The human cost was significant: at least 22 people were killed according to the authorities’ own figures; civil society monitors counted 30 dead and more than 1,500 arrested. Researchers have documented more than 70 episodes across 32 countries since 2014, with at least one case each year. Access Now’s KeepItOn coalition counted independently and arrived at the same number.

States typically employ two distinct tactics: prosecuting individuals for their online speech or disabling the network entirely to prevent collective action. While the former relies on cybercrime or false-news laws, the latter serves as a tool to disperse assemblies before they can form.

Legal arguments often focus on freedom of expression, but this approach misses the broader issue of assembly rights. While Article 9 of the African Charter protects expression, Article 11 specifically covers the right to assemble. Courts frequently overlook the latter, failing to recognize that internet access is essential for organizing peaceful gatherings.
To protect digital rights, advocates must shift their focus toward assembly claims, ensuring that courts address the state's duty to facilitate, rather than suppress, digital connectivity.

pages.text: The intersection of digital connectivity and civil unrest in Africa has prompted governments to weaponize network infrastructure as a means of suppressing dissent. This trend was starkly illustrated in July 2025, when Angola implemented its first national internet shutdown in response to fuel price protests.
pages.caption: Kenya High Court building

imageProvenance.credit: Kenya Judiciary building. Image by Wing via Wikimedia Commons ().

pages.text: The consequences were severe; at least 22 people were killed according to the authorities’ own figures; civil society monitors counted 30 dead and more than 1,500 arrested. Systematic tracking of telecommunications law reveals a persistent pattern of interference. Since 2014, there have been more than 70 episodes across 32 countries, with cases recorded every year.

Access Now’s KeepItOn coalition counted independently and arrived at the same number. Governments generally oscillate between two strategies: targeting individual dissenters through cybercrime statutes or executing broad network disruptions to neutralize collective mobilization. The latter is not merely a restriction on speech but a tactical maneuver to prevent the formation of assemblies.

Current legal discourse remains tethered to Article 9 of the African Charter, which pertains to freedom of expression. However, this framework is insufficient for addressing the systemic nature of shutdowns. Article 11, which guarantees the right to peaceful assembly, provides a more robust legal basis for challenging these disruptions.

Despite the existence of international standards, such as the UN’s General Comment 37, regional courts have been hesitant to rule on assembly claims, often defaulting to narrower arguments regarding expression or economic rights. For digital protest to be effectively protected, litigators must explicitly invoke the state's positive obligation to facilitate assembly.
Treating non-compliance as an enforcement failure rather than a legal ambiguity is essential to curbing the state's reach into the digital sphere.
